fetched_contents.text: A subject relative clause preference in a split-ergative language: ERP evidence from Georgian Introduction It is a well-known observation that subject relative clauses are more common cross-linguistically than object relative clauses (Keenan and Comrie, 1977). One possible explanation put forth by Keenan and Comrie (1977) to account for this pattern is that subject relative clauses are easier to process in online comprehension. Since then, a large body of experimental work has emerged investigating the relative difficulty of processing subject and object relative clauses. Using a wide variety of psycholinguistic measures, a subject processing advantage in relative clauses has been clearly observed for English (self-paced reading time: King & Just, 1991; ERP: King & Kutas, 1995; PET: Stromswold et al., 1996, Caplan et al., 1998, Caplan et al., 1999, Caplan et al., 2000; fMRI: Just et al., 1996, Caplan et al., 2002, Cooke et al., 2002, Constable et al., 2004, Chen et al., 2006, Caplan et al., 2008; eye-tracking: Traxler et al., 2002), as well as for other languages including Dutch (Frazier 1987), German (Mecklinger et al., 1995, Schriefers et al., 1995, Münte et al., 1997, Bader and Meng, 1999, Schwartz, 2007), French (Frauenfelder et al., 1980, Holmes and O’Regan, 1981, Cohen and Mehler, 1996), Hebrew (Friedmann and Novogrodsky, 2004, Arnon, 2005), Turkish (Kahraman et al., 2010), and Russian (Polinsky, 2011, Levy et al., 2013). Theories of relative clause processing that have been put forth to explain these results have tended to focus either on the linear/temporal distance between the filler (in this case, the head noun) and the gap (inside the relative clause), or, alternatively, on the grammatical function of the relativized noun, whereby relativization on subjects is inherently easier to process. One obvious way to distinguish between these sets of theories is to look at languages that have prenominal relative clauses. In these languages, distance between the gap and filler will be shorter in object relative clauses, so if the subject processing advantage seen in languages with postnominal relative clauses, like English, is due to linear/temporal distance between the filler and gap, then we would expect object relative clauses to be easier. If, on the other hand, relativization on subjects is universally easier to process, then such languages should show the familiar preference for subject relative clauses. The subject gap processing advantage has been consistently replicated in two languages with prenominal relative clauses: Japanese (self-paced reading time: Kanno and Nakamura, 2001, Miyamoto and Nakamura, 2003, Ishizuka et al., 2003; ERP: Ueno & Garnsey, 2008) and Korean (self-paced reading time: Kwon et al., 2006, Kwon, 2008; eye-tracking: Kwon et al., 2010; ERP: Kwon et al., 2013), seeming to argue against a simple filler-gap distance account. For Chinese, however, mixed results have been reported: Hsiao and Gibson’s initial (2003) report that Mandarin showed a preference for object relative clauses, supporting the linear distance account, has been followed up by a rich set of experimental studies, some of which replicate the object-relative clause preference (self-paced reading time: Lin and Garnsey, 2007, Chen et al., 2008, Lin, 2010, Gibson and Wu, 2013; maze-task: Qiao et al., 2012), some of which rather indicate a preference for subject relative clauses (self-paced reading time: Lin & Bever, 2006, Chen et al., 2010; Vasishth et al., 2013, Xu et al., 2019), and some of which argue that both SRCs and ORCs show distinct processing costs in different ERP measures (Bulut et al., 2018). For Cantonese, an object relative clause preference has been reported for child language, at least based on production (Yip & Matthews, 2007). Although debate continues over how best to understand the variability observed across the Mandarin and Cantonese data, on the whole what seems clear from work on the processing of prenominal relative clauses is that (a) facilitated processing for subject gaps cannot be wholly attributed to the linear distance between the gap position and the filler (given the residual subject relative clause preference observed in the Japanese and Korean studies) and (b) other factors must also impact the ease of relative clause processing, given the differences in the processing profile for Mandarin/Cantonese (at the least, in the greater variability observed across studies). A recent set of careful picture-matching experiments in the verb-first language of Chamorro, which allows both prenominal and postnominal relative clauses, reinforces this picture (Wagers, Borja, & Chung, 2018). By examining interpretations of SRC/ORC ambiguous sentences in Chamorro, Wagers et al., found that the same participants that show a strong SRC interpretation bias for postnominal relative clauses, can flip to a slight ORC bias in prenominal relative clauses. This finding clearly demonstrates that SRC vs ORC preferences can shifted by other factors, such as linear order. However, Wagers et al., also found evidence that initiation times were faster overall for trials in which an SRC was chosen, and that in unambiguous postnominal relative clauses participants were more likely to make errors in which they interpreted an unambiguous ORC as an SRC. They argue that relative clause processing profiles are driven by both the desire to interpret the gap as rapidly as possible (linear distance) and a desire to link gaps to subjects (subject preference), and that these factors can interact differently depending on language-specific properties. Yet another dimension of cross-linguistic variation has to do with the encoding of subjects. Morphological cues can affect subject advantage in relative clauses by making the subject more or less interpretable, by signaling grammatical function, and by interacting with the processing mechanisms that underlie the advantage itself. The most relevant cues in this context are marking, case, agreement, and subject-encoding differences across languages, because they help readers identify whether the gap is subject-like or object-like, and whether the clause’s head noun is likely to be the antecedent of the relative clause [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F1].

The evidence suggests that morphological cues are especially important when languages differ in how they encode subjecthood. In ergative-absolutive alignment, the subject of an intransitive verb behaves like the object of a transitive verb, so the morphological profile of a noun phrase can be much less diagnostic about grammatical function than in nominative-accusative languages [N2-R3][N2-R4]. In this setting, the absence of a strong subject marker may reduce the interpretive advantage of a subject gap, because the cue that normally identifies a subject is weaker or absent [N2-R5]. Conversely, when subject cues are more salient, the subject becomes easier to interpret, which can reinforce a subject advantage in relative clause processing [N2-R1].

Morphological cues can also neutralize or create a disadvantage for the subject advantage. One way this happens is by shifting processing load. For example, if a language has a marked ergative case, the claim is that languages with ergative subjects will prefer object relative clauses headed by the unmarked absolutive, because the marked case makes the ergative subject less salient as the head noun [N2-R5]. This is a classic neutralization mechanism: a marked cue may reduce the advantage by making the subject harder to identify, or by making object relatives more attractive because their head noun is in the unmarked case. Another way cues can neutralize an advantage is through cue competition. In the review evidence, the subject advantage is described as a cross-linguistic pattern, but the same evidence also notes that morphological and syntactic preferences for absolutive objects can counteract a subject preference associated with relative clauses [N2-R2]. So cues can either reinforce a preference or override it, depending on whether they support or contradict the expected grammatical function of the gap.

The evidence also shows that cues can create a disadvantage for the subject advantage. If a language has overt morphological case or agreement that signals objecthood more strongly than subjecthood, then the subject gap may become harder to interpret, which can reduce or reverse the advantage [N2-R2][N4-F1]. This is especially relevant in languages where subject encoding is not overt, such as Mandarin and Cantonese, where the evidence in the provided search results notes that these languages do not have overt morphological case [N1-F1]. In such cases, the lack of a subject marker may reduce the advantage, or even create a disadvantage, because readers have fewer cues to identify the subject as the antecedent of the relative clause [N1-F1].

Taken together, the evidence supports a clear mechanism: morphological cues shape subject advantage by signaling grammatical function, by affecting cue salience, and by interacting with the broader processing mechanisms that prefer subject gaps or object gaps. The strongest claim is that cues can neutralize an advantage when they counteract subject preference, and they can create a disadvantage when they make the subject harder to interpret [N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-F1].

The evidence for neutralization in ergative relative clauses is mixed but suggestive: the subject advantage does not always disappear, and it may disappear in certain contexts depending on how cues are encoded and how the clause is structured. The review and primary evidence indicate that subject-gap relative clauses are harder to process than object-gap ones in most languages, but recent work questions whether this holds in ergative languages like Georgian and split-ergative languages more generally [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. This is important because it implies that the subject advantage is not universal and can be neutralized when the grammatical system and relative clause structure differ from the nominative-accusative case [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Neutralization is measured experimentally and corporally in different ways. The experimental evidence in the provided search results includes ERP and self-paced reading measures, which are particularly useful for detecting processing difficulty and interpretive bias [N1-F1][N3-R4][N3-R5]. In the split-ergative study, ERP and self-paced reading results showed a large anterior negativity and slower reading times when a relative clause was disambiguated to an object interpretation, suggesting that the processing profile can shift depending on how the clause is interpreted [N3-R4]. In contrast, corpus evidence is also relevant because the search results include a large-scale corpus analysis indicating that pronominal object relative clauses are significantly more frequent than pronominal subject relative clauses [N5-R1]. This frequency pattern may reflect a neutralization of subject preference in the corpus, because it shows that object relatives are more common, which can be interpreted as a weakening or reversal of the subject advantage.

Language-specific patterns support or contradict the effect in different ways. In the provided evidence, Georgian is presented as a split-ergative language where a subject relative clause preference was examined, and the results were described as showing ERP and self-paced reading effects that are consistent with the broader claim that subject-gap relative clauses are harder to process than object-gap ones [N3-R4]. This suggests that in some ergative contexts, the subject advantage remains detectable, but not necessarily in the same form as in nominative-accusative languages. In contrast, the evidence also notes that morphological and syntactic preferences for absolutive objects can counteract a subject preference associated with relative clauses, which implies that neutralization can occur when object cues are stronger or more salient [N2-R2]. For Mandarin and Cantonese, the evidence is even more explicit: these languages do not have overt morphological case, so the subject advantage may be weaker or absent because there is less cue support for subjecthood [N1-F1]. This is a direct contradiction to the idea of a universal subject advantage, because the absence of a subject marker can neutralize the advantage.

Overall, the evidence supports a conditional conclusion: the subject advantage can disappear or weaken in ergative relative clauses when morphological cues favor objecthood, when the clause structure is head-initial or prenominal, or when the language lacks overt subject markers. At the same time, the evidence does not support a complete disappearance in all ergative languages; instead, it suggests that the effect is context-sensitive and language-specific [N2-R2][N3-R2][N3-R4][N5-R1]. The most reliable neutralization evidence comes from experimental measures showing slower reading and larger processing effects for object interpretations, while corpus evidence points to a frequency asymmetry that may also indicate neutralization [N3-R4][N5-R1].

Subject advantage in relative clauses refers to the observation that subject-gap relative clauses are generally easier to process than object-gap relative clauses. The evidence from the provided search results and review material shows that this is a well-established cross-linguistic pattern: studies from many languages consistently report that subject relative clauses are easier to process than object relatives [N4-R2][N4-R3][N5-R2]. In experimental work, this is usually measured through self-paced reading, eye-tracking, ERP, and other psycholinguistic methods, and the results are interpreted as evidence that the parser prefers subject gaps or that subject gaps are easier to interpret [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-F3].

The core mechanism is that the subject is treated as the preferred gap in relative clause processing. The review evidence explicitly states that the subject advantage is a cross-linguistic phenomenon and that the most common explanation is that subject-gap relative clauses are easier to process than object-gap ones [N4-R2]. Theoretical proposals in the evidence include the accessibility hierarchy, which claims that grammatical functions are universally ordered in a way that makes subjects more accessible than objects [N4-F1], and the perspective shift hypothesis, which argues that subjects determine the perspective of a clause and that processing a subject relative clause entails no shift, while object relative clauses induce a shift to a new subject [N4-F1]. These theories are important because they explain why subject gaps may be preferred: they are either more accessible, require less processing shift, or are more efficient in some parsing strategy.

Ergative languages differ from nominative-accusative languages in how they encode subjecthood. In ergative-absolutive alignment, the subject of an intransitive verb behaves like the object of a transitive verb, so subject marking is not uniform across transitivity [N2-R3]. In contrast, in nominative-accusative alignment, the subject is typically marked by a nominative case, and object is marked by an accusative case, making subjecthood more salient and easier to cue [N2-R3][N2-R4]. This difference matters for subject advantage because the presence of a strong subject marker can reinforce the advantage, while the absence of such a marker can weaken or neutralize it [N2-R5][N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that some languages showing morphological ergativity in case and/or agreement also show ergative patterns in core syntactic domains, which means that the relationship between morphology and relative clause structure is not trivial [N2-R4].

Which relative clause structures are most relevant to the effect? The evidence points to head-initial, prenominal, and postnominal relative clauses. In the provided evidence, the subject gap processing advantage is said to be consistently replicated in two languages with prenominal relative clauses: Japanese and Korean [N1-F1]. That is important because it suggests that the advantage is not purely a postnominal effect and that it can persist even when the gap is closer to the head. The same evidence also notes that in some languages, such as Chinese, results are mixed and that the subject advantage cannot be wholly attributed to linear distance [N1-F1]. This implies that the most relevant relative clause structures are those that allow the parser to compare subject and object gaps, and that the effect is strongest when the morphological system supports a clear subject marker [N1-F1][N4-R2]. Overall, subject advantage matters because it is a central asymmetry in relative clause processing, and it is shaped by both grammatical function and the morphological cues that make the subject easier or harder to identify [N4-R2][N4-F1][N2-R3].

The theoretical and methodological constraints on the question are substantial. The evidence suggests that the best explanations are not a single universal theory but a combination of accessibility-based, expectation-based, and structural accounts. The review and primary evidence cite proposals such as the accessibility hierarchy, which posits that grammatical functions are universally ordered and that subjects are more accessible than objects [N4-F1]. It also cites expectation-based accounts, which suggest that processing is driven by the desire to interpret the gap as rapidly as possible and by the desire to link gaps to subjects [N4-F1]. The evidence further notes that Chinese relative clauses are an important test case for pitting expectation-based accounts against memory-based theories [N7-R2]. This shows that the phenomenon is best explained by a pluralistic framework rather than a single theory.

A major constraint is that experimental evidence can show the presence of effects, but it cannot always capture the full source or boundary conditions of the effect. The evidence includes self-paced reading, eye-tracking, ERP, and picture-matching experiments, all of which are useful for detecting processing difficulty and interpretive bias [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-F1][N5-F3]. However, the same evidence also highlights that results can be mixed or context-dependent. For example, the review notes that in Chinese, results are mixed and that the subject advantage cannot be wholly attributed to linear distance [N1-F1]. This is a methodological limitation: experiments can confirm the presence of an effect, but they may not isolate the exact mechanism, especially when multiple factors interact [N1-F1][N4-F1].

Corpus evidence is valuable but has its own limitations. The provided evidence includes a large-scale corpus analysis showing that pronominal object relative clauses are significantly more frequent than pronominal subject relative clauses [N5-R1]. This is important because frequency patterns can indicate a neutralization of the subject advantage or a preference for object relatives. However, corpus evidence is indirect: it can show what is common, but not necessarily why. The evidence also shows that corpus-based frequency is only one piece of evidence among many [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Another limitation is that corpora may not capture online processing or cue salience in the same way as experimental measures [N5-F3].

Language typology and cue salience are central to generalization. The evidence repeatedly shows that the subject advantage is not universal and depends on how grammatical functions are encoded. In ergative-absolutive alignment, the subject of an intransitive verb behaves like the object of a transitive verb, so subject marking is not uniform [N2-R3]. In nominative-accusative alignment, subjecthood is typically marked by a nominative case, which makes the cue stronger [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that the absence of overt morphological case in Mandarin and Cantonese weakens the subject advantage, because there are fewer cues to identify the subject [N1-F1]. This means that generalization is highly typology-sensitive: the more salient the subject cue, the stronger the advantage; the less salient the cue, the weaker or absent the advantage [N2-R3][N2-R4][N1-F1]. In short, the evidence supports a cautious conclusion: the observed effects are best explained by a combination of accessibility, expectation, and structural factors, but the effect is not universal and depends heavily on cue salience and language typology [N4-F1][N7-R2][N1-F1].

A cross-linguistic and typological comparison framework is essential for understanding how morphological cues interact with relative clause structure. The most important typological factors are morphological case marking, subject-encoding, alignment type, and linear clause order. The evidence shows that ergative-absolutive alignment is a key typological variable because it changes how subjecthood is encoded: the subject of an intransitive verb behaves like the object of a transitive verb [N2-R3]. This makes subject marking less uniform and more dependent on transitivity, which can weaken the subject advantage compared to nominative-accusative languages [N2-R3][N2-R4]. In contrast, nominative-accusative alignment typically marks subjects with a nominative case, making subjecthood more salient and easier to cue [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that languages such as Mandarin and Cantonese do not have overt morphological case, so subject encoding is weaker, and this can reduce or neutralize the subject advantage [N1-F1]. This shows that cue salience is a central typological factor: stronger subject cues reinforce the advantage, while weaker or absent cues reduce it [N2-R3][N1-F1].

Split-ergative vs. absolutive alignment changes the effect in important ways. The provided evidence includes a split-ergative study in Georgian and a broader discussion of split-ergative languages [N1-F1][N3-R4]. In split-ergative alignment, the ergative is marked in some syntactic domains, while absolutive alignment is more uniform. This matters because the presence of a marked ergative case can make the subject less salient as the head noun, which can neutralize the subject advantage [N2-R5]. At the same time, the evidence suggests that split-ergative languages may preserve some of the subject advantage, but the effect is not universal [N1-F1][N3-R2]. This indicates that the effect is not only a matter of whether a language is ergative or absolutive, but also of how subjecthood is marked and how the clause structure interacts with that marking [N1-F1][N2-R3].

Subject cue visibility interacts with relative clause structure in a predictable way. The evidence repeatedly points to prenominal and postnominal relative clauses as structurally relevant contexts [N1-F1]. In prenominal relative clauses, the gap is closer to the head, and the evidence suggests that the subject advantage cannot be wholly attributed to linear distance [N1-F1]. That means cue visibility matters not only in terms of whether the subject is marked, but also in terms of how the clause structure makes the gap easier or harder to identify. The same evidence also notes that in Chamorro, the same participants who show a strong SRC bias in postnominal relative clauses can flip to a slight ORC bias in prenominal relative clauses [N1-F1]. This shows that cue visibility interacts with clause structure: when the gap is closer and the cue system is weaker, object relatives may become more attractive [N1-F1]. In sum, the cross-linguistic framework is dominated by alignment type, case marking, subject-encoding strength, and clause order, with the clearest conclusion that cue visibility and typology shape the strength and direction of the subject advantage [N2-R3][N2-R4][N1-F1][N3-R2].

The central idea is that relative clause processing is shaped not only by the grammatical function of the gap, but by how visible that function is in morphology.

### 1) What subject advantage means, and why it matters in relative clauses

## How morphological cues affect the presence or neutralization of the subject advantage in ergative relative clauses

The evidence supports a nuanced answer: **morphological cues can reinforce, weaken, or neutralize the subject advantage in relative clauses, and the effect is especially sensitive to ergativity, clause structure, and cue salience** [N4-R2][N4-R3][N5-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The central idea is that relative clause processing is shaped not only by the grammatical function of the gap, but by how visible that function is in morphology.

### 1) What subject advantage means, and why it matters in relative clauses

Subject advantage refers to the observation that **subject-gap relative clauses are generally easier to process than object-gap relative clauses** [N4-R2][N4-R3][N5-R2]. In experimental work, this is usually measured through self-paced reading, eye-tracking, ERP, and other psycholinguistic methods, and the results are interpreted as evidence that the parser prefers subject gaps or that subject gaps are easier to interpret [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-F3]. The review evidence explicitly states that the subject advantage is a cross-linguistic phenomenon and that the most common explanation is that subject-gap relative clauses are easier to process than object-gap ones [N4-R2].

The theoretical background provided in the branch reports includes several proposals. One is the **accessibility hierarchy**, which claims that grammatical functions are universally ordered in a way that makes subjects more accessible than objects [N4-F1]. Another is the **perspective shift hypothesis**, which argues that subjects determine the perspective of a clause and that processing a subject relative clause entails no shift, while object relative clauses induce a shift to a new subject [N4-F1]. These theories matter because they explain why subject gaps may be preferred: they are either more accessible, require less processing shift, or are more efficient in some parsing strategy.

Ergative languages matter differently because they differ from nominative-accusative languages in how they encode subjecthood. In **ergative-absolutive alignment**, the subject of an intransitive verb behaves like the object of a transitive verb, so subject marking is not uniform across transitivity [N2-R3]. In contrast, in **nominative-accusative alignment**, the subject is typically marked by a nominative case, and object is marked by an accusative case, making subjecthood more salient and easier to cue [N2-R3][N2-R4]. This difference matters for subject advantage because the presence of a strong subject marker can reinforce the advantage, while the absence of such a marker can weaken or neutralize it [N2-R5][N1-F1].

The branch reports also emphasize that the most relevant relative clause structures are **head-initial, prenominal, and postnominal relative clauses**. The evidence points to prenominal relative clauses as especially important because the subject gap processing advantage has been consistently replicated in two languages with prenominal relative clauses: Japanese and Korean [N1-F1]. That is important because it suggests that the advantage is not purely a postnominal effect and can persist even when the gap is closer to the head. The same evidence also notes that in some languages, such as Chinese, results are mixed and that the subject advantage cannot be wholly attributed to linear distance [N1-F1]. So, the effect is strongest when the morphological system supports a clear subject marker, and it depends on how the clause is structured [N4-R2][N4-F1][N2-R3].

### 2) How morphological cues can affect subject advantage

The branch reports show that **morphological cues are especially relevant when they signal grammatical function, marking, case, agreement, and subject-encoding differences** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. These cues matter because they help readers identify whether the gap is subject-like or object-like and whether the clause’s head noun is likely to be the antecedent of the relative clause [N2-R1][N2-R2].

One mechanism is that **cues make the subject more or less interpretable**. In languages where subject marking is strong, the subject becomes easier to interpret, which can reinforce the subject advantage [N2-R1][N2-R2]. In languages where subject encoding is weaker or absent, the subject becomes harder to interpret, which can weaken or even create a disadvantage for the subject advantage [N2-R5][N1-F1]. The branch report also notes that morphological and syntactic preferences for absolutive objects can counteract a subject preference associated with relative clauses, showing that cues can override the expected grammatical function of the gap [N2-R2].

Another mechanism is that **cues can neutralize an advantage or create a disadvantage**. The branch report explicitly states that cues can neutralize an advantage when they counteract subject preference, and they can create a disadvantage when they make the subject harder to interpret [N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-F1]. This is especially relevant in ergative languages, where the marked ergative case may reduce the advantage by making the ergative subject less salient as the head noun, while the unmarked absolutive may make object relatives more attractive [N2-R5]. This is a classic neutralization mechanism: a marked cue may reduce the advantage by making the subject harder to identify, or by making object relatives more attractive because their head noun is in the unmarked case [N2-R5].

### 3) Evidence for neutralization in ergative relative clauses

The evidence for neutralization is **mixed but suggestive**. The review and primary evidence indicate that subject-gap relative clauses are harder to process than object-gap ones in most languages, but recent work questions whether this holds in ergative languages like Georgian and split-ergative languages more generally [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. This is important because it implies that the subject advantage is not universal and can be neutralized when the grammatical system and relative clause structure differ from the nominative-accusative case [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Neutralization is measured experimentally and corporally in different ways. The branch reports point to **ERP and self-paced reading measures** as especially useful for detecting processing difficulty and interpretive bias [N1-F1][N3-R4][N3-R5]. In the split-ergative study, ERP and self-paced reading results showed a large anterior negativity and slower reading times when a relative clause was disambiguated to an object interpretation, suggesting that the processing profile can shift depending on how the clause is interpreted [N3-R4]. In contrast, **corpus evidence** is also relevant because the search results include a large-scale corpus analysis indicating that pronominal object relative clauses are significantly more frequent than pronominal subject relative clauses [N5-R1]. This frequency pattern may reflect a neutralization of subject preference in the corpus, because it shows that object relatives are more common, which can be interpreted as a weakening or reversal of the subject advantage [N5-R1].

Language-specific patterns support or contradict the effect in different ways. In the provided evidence, **Georgian is presented as a split-ergative language where a subject relative clause preference was examined**, and the results were described as showing ERP and self-paced reading effects consistent with the broader claim that subject-gap relative clauses are harder to process than object-gap ones [N3-R4]. This suggests that in some ergative contexts, the subject advantage remains detectable, but not necessarily in the same form as in nominative-accusative languages. In contrast, the evidence also notes that morphological and syntactic preferences for absolutive objects can counteract a subject preference associated with relative clauses, implying that neutralization can occur when object cues are stronger or more salient [N2-R2]. For **Mandarin and Cantonese**, the evidence is even more explicit: these languages do not have overt morphological case, so the subject advantage may be weaker or absent because there are fewer cues to identify the subject [N1-F1]. This is a direct contradiction to the idea of a universal subject advantage, because the absence of a subject marker can neutralize the advantage.

### 4) Theoretical and methodological constraints

The evidence suggests that the best explanations are **not a single universal theory but a combination of accessibility-based, expectation-based, and structural accounts** [N4-F1][N7-R2]. The review and primary evidence cite proposals such as the accessibility hierarchy, expectation-based accounts, and structural accounts, showing that the phenomenon is best explained by a pluralistic framework rather than a single theory [N4-F1][N7-R2].

A major methodological constraint is that **experimental evidence can show the presence of effects, but it cannot always capture the full source or boundary conditions**. The evidence includes self-paced reading, eye-tracking, ERP, and picture-matching experiments, all of which are useful for detecting processing difficulty and interpretive bias [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-F1][N5-F3]. However, the same evidence also highlights that results can be mixed or context-dependent. For example, the review notes that in Chinese, results are mixed and that the subject advantage cannot be wholly attributed to linear distance [N1-F1]. This is a methodological limitation: experiments can confirm the presence of an effect, but they may not isolate the exact mechanism, especially when multiple factors interact [N1-F1][N4-F1].

Corpus evidence is valuable but has its own limitations. The branch reports show that **a large-scale corpus analysis indicates that pronominal object relative clauses are significantly more frequent than pronominal subject relative clauses** [N5-R1]. This is important because frequency patterns can indicate a neutralization of the subject advantage or a preference for object relatives. However, corpus evidence is indirect: it can show what is common, but not necessarily why. The evidence also shows that corpus-based frequency is only one piece of evidence among many [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Another limitation is that corpora may not capture online processing or cue salience in the same way as experimental measures [N5-F3].

Language typology and cue salience are central to generalization. The evidence repeatedly shows that the subject advantage is **not universal** and depends on how grammatical functions are encoded. In **ergative-absolutive alignment**, subject marking is not uniform across transitivity, which can weaken the subject advantage [N2-R3]. In **nominative-accusative alignment**, subjecthood is typically marked by a nominative case, making subjecthood more salient and easier to cue [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence also notes that the absence of overt morphological case in Mandarin and Cantonese weakens the subject advantage, because there are fewer cues to identify the subject [N1-F1]. This means that generalization is highly typology-sensitive: the more salient the subject cue, the stronger the advantage; the less salient the cue, the weaker or absent the advantage [N2-R3][N2-R4][N1-F1]. In short, the observed effects are best explained by a combination of accessibility, expectation, and structural factors, but the effect is not universal and depends heavily on cue salience and language typology [N4-F1][N7-R2][N1-F1].

### 5) Cross-linguistic and typological comparison framework

A cross-linguistic and typological comparison framework is essential for understanding how morphological cues interact with relative clause structure. The most important typological factors are **morphological case marking, subject-encoding, alignment type, and linear clause order** [N2-R3][N2-R4][N1-F1][N3-R2]. The branch reports show that **ergative-absolutive alignment** is a key typological variable because it changes how subjecthood is encoded: the subject of an intransitive verb behaves like the object of a transitive verb [N2-R3]. This makes subject marking less uniform and more dependent on transitivity, which can weaken the subject advantage compared to nominative-accusative languages [N2-R3][N2-R4].

**Split-ergative vs. absolutive alignment** changes the effect in important ways. The branch reports include a split-ergative study in Georgian and a broader discussion of split-ergative languages [N1-F1][N3-R4]. In split-ergative alignment, the ergative is marked in some syntactic domains, while absolutive alignment is more uniform. This matters because the presence of a marked ergative case can make the subject less salient as the head noun, which can neutralize the subject advantage [N2-R5]. At the same time, the evidence suggests that split-ergative languages may preserve some of the subject advantage, but the effect is not universal [N1-F1][N3-R2]. This indicates that the effect is not only a matter of whether a language is ergative or absolutive, but also of how subjecthood is marked and how the clause structure interacts with that marking [N1-F1][N2-R3].

**Subject cue visibility interacts with relative clause structure** in a predictable way. The evidence repeatedly points to prenominal and postnominal relative clauses as structurally relevant contexts [N1-F1]. In prenominal relative clauses, the gap is closer to the head, and the evidence suggests that the subject advantage cannot be wholly attributed to linear distance [N1-F1]. That means cue visibility matters not only in terms of whether the subject is marked, but also in terms of how the clause structure makes the gap easier or harder to identify. The same evidence also notes that in Chamorro, the same participants who show a strong SRC bias in postnominal relative clauses can flip to a slight ORC bias in prenominal relative clauses [N1-F1]. This shows that cue visibility interacts with clause structure: when the gap is closer and the cue system is weaker, object relatives may become more attractive [N1-F1].

### 6) Bottom line

Overall, the answer is **conditional**: morphological cues can affect the subject advantage in ergative relative clauses by making the subject more or less interpretable, by signaling grammatical function, and by interacting with broader processing mechanisms [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F1]. The subject advantage does not disappear in all ergative languages; it can weaken, neutralize, or even reverse depending on whether the cues support or contradict the expected grammatical function of the gap [N2-R2][N3-R2][N3-R4][N5-R1]. The most reliable evidence comes from experimental measures showing slower reading and larger processing effects for object interpretations, while corpus evidence points to a frequency asymmetry that may also indicate neutralization [N3-R4][N5-R1]. Theoretical and methodological constraints remind us that the effect is best explained by a pluralistic account rather than a single universal theory, and that generalization is highly sensitive to cue salience and language typology [N4-F1][N7-R2][N1-F1].

In short: **morphological cues can reinforce, weaken, or neutralize the subject advantage in ergative relative clauses, depending on how the subject is marked, how the clause is structured, and how the language system balances accessibility, expectation, and structural load** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F1][N1-F1][N3-R4].
